argument_text: And therefore — the unmade I, real, self-lit in form — the supreme Lord pulses and shines by the power of the supreme Lady, taking the shape of the world from Śiva down to clay. This very shining is His making of the world — and the world's being alive. But what kind of "made" is the world — made as something different from Him, or as nothing different? If different, His freedom breaks; if not different, how is it made at all? The answer: without another's light the world cannot even be noticed, let alone come into its own — its coming to wear a shining body, leaning on His ground, is exactly what "made" means here. Māyā's own freedom puts difference on display, so the world is handled as different while being nothing different. "Made," in the end, means nothing but shining-by-Him. Formed this way, the world is nothing apart from Maheśvara the maker, who is shining-formed. For if what is known stood apart, it could not shine, and no shining could reach it — there would be nothing at all, and all the traffic of taking and giving would collapse. And if the world is nothing apart from the Lord, must He not be stained by resemblance to a merely shining world — veiled by it? Rather the would-be veil destroys itself: gained even within the self, veiling the light would unmake itself. By this world, then, the Lord's light-formed nature is never veiled — the world, given rest by His shining, has become His very life-breath. How could it throttle Him — and throttling Him, itself go on standing?
